In brief

Joyce's portrait of a martyred hero mocks the Citizen's blather about "Robert Emmet and die for your country, the Tommy Moore touch about Sara Curran and she's far from the land," but the parody does not use these names. It calls the man only "the central figure of the tragedy" and his fiancée the "bride elect"—i.e., the person he has chosen to become his bride. This expression was used more commonly in Victorian and Edwardian times than today. Still, it seems odd that no commentator in the last hundred years has heard in it an allusion to Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado. Fans of that work will inevitably think of the famous comic duet in which the emperor is upstaged by his "daughter-in-law elect." Something similar happens in Joyce's scene, as the victim, introduced only a moment before, is upstaged by a flamboyantly confident woman.

At more length

In act 2 the Mikado enters for the first time accompanied by Katisha, the formidable elderly woman whom he has chosen as a wife for his son Nanki-Poo (to her delight, and the son's dismay). In a duet the Mikado asserts his absolute authority, and she asserts rather more:

Mik. From every kind of man
Obedience I expect;
I'm the Emperor of Japan—
Kat. And I'm his daughter-in-law elect!
He'll marry his son
(He's only got one)
To his daughter-in-law elect!
Mik. My morals have been declared
Particularly correct;
Kat. But they're nothing at all, compared
With those of his daughter-in-law elect!
Mik. In a fatherly kind of way
I govern each tribe and sect,
All cheerfully own my sway—
Kat. Except his daughter-in-law elect!
As tough as a bone,
With a will of her own,
Is his daughter-in-law elect!
Mik. My nature is love and light—
My freedom from all defect—
Kat. Is insignificant quite,
Compared with his daughter-in-law elect!

After some of these exchanges the Chorus, led by Katisha, sings the refrain:

Bow— Bow—
To his daughter-in-law elect!

Katisha too is a "bride elect," and she treats that honor as political capital. No sooner has the Mikado taken the stage for the first time than his chosen daughter steals it from him. The same thing happens in Joyce's execution scene. As soon as the victim appears his chosen bride swoops in and steals the scene. She may be "blushing" and have a "willowy form," but this force of nature is seen to "burst her way through the serried ranks of the bystanders." Flinging herself on the victim and passionately kissing every part of his body she can reach, she swears her undying love, recounts tales of their childhood together, calls forth oceans of tears from the onlookers, and then, in a supreme act of upstaging, finds a new fiancé—one deeply embedded in the English power structure. For both women, romance seems subordinate to more worldly considerations.

The intertextual fabric runs still deeper. The Mikado is built on a plot of state punishment. The first act proceeds from an imperial decree that all flirtation will be punished by decapitation. In the second act, after disentangling himself from the clutches of his maniacally ambitious daughter-to-be, the Mikado announces that he will be imposing some lesser punishments. As evidence that "A more humane Mikado never did in Japan exist," he describes some ingeniously sadistic but non-fatal tortures that will make "the punishment fit the crime." Since Joyce's dramatic scene too features ingenious state-sanctioned tortures, an executioner specializing in decapitation, a pair of lovers, and death sentences not yet carried out, it seems unlikely that he dreamed it up without the strains of Gilbert and Sullivan's operetta playing in his mind.

For the crowning element of his story, though, he turned from fiction to real life. The romantic image of Sarah Curran created by Thomas Moore's song always sat somewhat uneasily with the fact of her having accepted a new proposal of marriage after Emmet's death. Joyce drives a Mack truck through that opening.

John Hunt 2026
